description: We are a diverse team of students from Aristotle University of Thessaloniki (AUTH), united by our enthusiasm for learning, innovation, and collaboration. We are eager to exchange ideas, develop new skills, and work together on creative and impactful projects.
summary:
EarthDance is a web app that turns NASA–ISRO NISAR radar into an early-warning tool for Greece’s protected lakes. We built it on Lake Koroneia, a Natura 2000 and Ramsar wetland near Thessaloniki. The lake dried out completely in 2002, and in 2013 the EU Court ruled that Greece had failed to protect it.

Optical satellites are blind under cloud on most winter days. NISAR’s L-band radar sees through cloud, day and night. Calm water looks dark to the radar, so every pass measures the lake’s surface area. EarthDance combines these measurements with weather data in a simple water-balance model, fitted to 14 real measurements, and forecasts when the lake will fall below its limit, with an uncertainty range. It then gives the Region a plain-language alert: what we measured, what is coming, and what to do. Users can test “what if” scenarios and ask questions, and every answer is built from the data.

This matters because today the authorities act after the damage. Weeks of early warning let them protect the wetland and plan irrigation before a fine follows.
details:
Project details

What it does and how it works
EarthDance turns NISAR L-band radar into decisions for the people who manage Greece’s protected lakes. It has three views:

  • Explore: a map timeline of the radar passes, with a switch between the optical view (Sentinel-2, often clouded) and the radar view. Hover over any point to see the value in dB and a plain explanation.
  • Story: six short chapters for the public, from clouds to radar, water, reeds, sinking ground and decisions.
  • Status: a daily briefing for the Region. It shows the lake’s water area over time, a forecast with a “Today” line and an uncertainty band, and an alert in three lines: what we measured, what is coming, what to do. It also has a what-if scenario for rain and irrigation, an “Ask EarthDance” panel and a one-click PDF report.

The pipeline works in four steps:

  1. Download NISAR L2 GCOV (HH) passes from ASF DAAC.
  2. Map water as dark pixels (≤ −18 dB) inside the lake. Passes from a steep orbit and wind-roughened passes are left out.
  3. Fit a water-balance model (dS = a·rain − k·ET0; area = A_max·S^q) to the 14 measured areas.
  4. Run it with real weather up to today, then with 33 scenarios built from the weather of 2015–2025.

Its typical error is ±1.7 km². In a back-test that hid the last month of data, it warned about five weeks before the lake crossed its limit.

Benefits and intended impact
Authorities act months earlier instead of after the damage. That means:

  • fewer EU infringement risks and fines
  • protected habitats and birds
  • irrigation planned in spring, not in August

The tool costs almost nothing to run (static site, free data), and a new lake is one configuration file.

Tools

  • Front end: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with MapLibre GL for the map and Chart.js for the charts.
  • Processing: Python with rasterio, NumPy, SciPy and Pillow.
  • Data: NISAR L2 GCOV (NASA–ISRO, via ASF DAAC), Sentinel-2 HLS, Open-Meteo (ERA5 reanalysis and forecast) and Esri World Imagery as the base map. No special hardware.

Creativity

  • The physics is explained in plain words right on the map.
  • The lake “breathes” on a timeline.
  • “Ask EarthDance” answers from templates filled with the model’s numbers, so it never invents a figure.
  • A Real/Demo switch keeps every number honest.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about data: reeds, ground motion and soil moisture run on a clearly labelled demo set until those NISAR products are released for the site.
  • Uncertainty: forecasts are shown as ranges, not single numbers.
  • Users: the tool is built for non-expert officials.
  • Practical use: it has an offline weather fallback, works on phones and is available in Greek and English.
